title: Shiva's weapon and its rule
hookLine: Shiva gives Arjuna his own weapon with a warning, the guardians of the world add theirs, and a chariot comes down for him
carry: god-given power is bound by dharma

cards: What does a god give a man who just tried to kill him? Arjuna is on his knees, bruised, asking forgiveness. The hunter's disguise has fallen away, and Shiva stands before him with Uma at his side.
The first thing Shiva does isn't a lecture. He hands back the bow. Gandiva, the one he snatched in the fight, returns to Arjuna's hands.
Then Shiva says: ask for what you want.

teach.b: There's no anger in Shiva at all. He touches Arjuna, and his wounds and exhaustion are gone.

Then Arjuna asks for what he climbed the mountain for: Shiva's own weapon, the one called Pashupata. Shiva gives it to him, and teaches him how to use it. But he adds a warning, and it's the heart of the scene.
This weapon must never be hurled at a human foe, and never at a weaker one. Used wrongly, it could destroy the world. Shiva's own weapon comes with Shiva's own limit.

teach.h: THE GUARDIANS OF THE WORLD ARRIVE.
teach.b: Then the sky fills with visitors: the guardians of the world. Varuna, lord of the waters; Kubera, lord of wealth; Yama, lord of death; each offers Arjuna a weapon of his own.
Last comes Indra, the father who tested him in disguise. A chariot will come for you, Indra says, to carry you up to my city. Now the teaching.
In Hindu stories, divine power is never just power. It's given to protect dharma, the right order of things, and the weak inside it, and it comes with a rule.
That's how Hindus are often taught to read the weapons in the pictures at home: Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, the weapons the gods gave Durga for her many arms. They guard; they don't bully.
For today: whatever strength you've been given, a quick mind, a loud voice, a little authority, comes with Shiva's rule attached. Never against someone weaker.

how: In Hindu storytelling, Shiva's gift of the Pashupata weapon to Arjuna is remembered together with its warning, and the episode is honored by devotees of Shiva as a sign of the god's grace to a devoted seeker.

games.q: Sam sees Nani's picture of Durga, a weapon in each of her many arms, and asks if Hindu gods are violent. by today's story, what fits?
o: yes, the gods love a good fight.
the weapons guard dharma and the weak. Shiva even gave Arjuna his own weapon with a rule: never against someone weaker.
they're decoration; they don't mean anything.
games.why: in Hindu stories, divine power comes bound to dharma: Shiva's Pashupata was never to be used on a human foe or a weaker one.

practice: Bring to mind one strength you have, a skill, a sharp tongue, a position, a way with people, and breathe it in as a gift.
Breathe out with Shiva's warning, never against someone weaker, and let the question sit: where might that strength need a limit? If you pray, give thanks for that gift and ask to use it well.

wordCard.voice: Arjuna's austerities. They end with healing, the Pashupata weapon from Shiva, and a warning never to turn it on the weak.

orig.note: Sanskrit pāśupata: belonging to Pashupati, 'lord of creatures', a name of Shiva; the name of his weapon.

carryVoice: Your line: God-given power is bound by dharma. Shiva's own weapon came with Shiva's own rule. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Kairata Parva (Shiva returns Gandiva, heals Arjuna, grants the Pashupata with a warning; the guardians of the world give weapons; Indra promises a chariot)
Divine weapons as protectors of dharma: the gods arm Durga (Devi Mahatmya, chapter 2); Shiva's trident and Vishnu's discus in common iconography
